title: How Neural Stem Cells Keep Making Cells

scenes.visual: Title card: How Neural Stem Cells Keep Making Cells. Introduce the renewing neuroblast and its differentiating progeny.

scenes.tts: A neural stem cell has two jobs. Stay a stem cell, and make cells that differentiate. Asymmetric division lets it do both. In the fly, a neural stem cell is called a neuroblast. In most neuroblasts, the large daughter stays a stem cell. The small daughter is a ganglion mother cell. It divides once more to make two neurons or glia. This way, the neuroblast keeps making new cells without using up the stem cell.

scenes.visual: Show a type I fly neuroblast dividing along a vertical apical-basal axis. Label the large apical daughter neuroblast and the smaller basal daughter ganglion mother cell. Follow the smaller daughter through one division into two neurons or glia, while the retained neuroblast repeats the cycle. Keep renewal and differentiating output visible together.

scenes.tts: How does the cell sort the daughters? Polarity marks a top and a bottom. Par proteins and Inscuteable gather at the top. Inscuteable recruits Pins. Pins, with other proteins including Mud, lines the spindle up from top to bottom. The protein a P K C keeps Numb off the top. Numb, Prospero and Brat end up at the bottom. Division hands this cargo to the small daughter. There, Prospero enters the nucleus and shuts down genes for self renewal and division.

scenes.visual: Show the type I neuroblast before division, apical at top and basal at bottom. Label the apical Par complex and Inscuteable; show recruitment of Pins and a link through spindle-orientation machinery including Mud to spindle microtubules. Align the spindle vertically. Show aPKC excluding Numb from the apical cortex. At the basal crescent, distinguish Numb with its own adaptor from Miranda carrying Prospero and Brat. Cleavage separates the large apical neuroblast from the small basal ganglion mother cell. Move Prospero into the latter nucleus and dim self-renewal and division gene labels.

scenes.tts: Numb shows how inherited cargo changes fate. Take the fly bristle precursor. Numb forms a crescent and passes to one daughter only. There it blocks Notch, a receptor that carries signals between touching cells. The sister can still hear Notch.

scenes.visual: Explicitly switch from the neuroblast to a fly sensory organ precursor. Orient its division within the epithelial plane, along the head-to-tail axis. Preserve yellow Numb, teal Notch and red inhibition. Show the Numb crescent inherited by one daughter, blocking Notch reception only there.

scenes.tts: The Numb daughter takes the inner branch, leading to the neuron and sheath. Its sister takes the outer branch, leading to the hair and socket. Here both branches differentiate. Notch chooses between their fates.

scenes.visual: Show a simplified bristle branch-choice diagram: Numb-positive, Notch-off inner branch leads to neuron and sheath; Numb-negative, Notch-on outer branch leads to hair and socket. Label it simplified branches; use branching paths rather than depicting a direct single division into each mature pair. Make clear that both branches differentiate.

scenes.tts: Now test that rule. Remove Numb, and both daughters take the outer fate. The lineage makes four outer support cells and no neuron or sheath. Give Numb to both daughters, and both take the inner branch. Neurons and sheath cells form, but no bristle.

scenes.visual: Two compact bristle perturbation panels: no Numb gives two outer branches and four outer support cells, sockets, with no neuron or sheath. Numb in both first-division daughters gives two inner branches leading to neurons and sheath cells, with no hair or socket. Keep these bristle outcomes separate from neuroblast renewal.

scenes.tts: Back in the fly brain, failed fate control can cause overgrowth. The daughter may keep behaving like a stem cell. Prospero and Brat guard different cells. Without Prospero, tumours arise from ganglion mother cells. Without Brat, they arise mainly from intermediate progenitors in type two lineages. These progenitors normally divide several times, each time making a ganglion mother cell.
scenes.narration: Back in the fly brain, failed fate control can cause overgrowth. The daughter may keep behaving like a stem cell. Prospero and Brat guard different cells. Without Prospero, tumours arise from ganglion mother cells. Without Brat, they arise mainly from intermediate progenitors in type II lineages. These progenitors normally divide several times, each time making a ganglion mother cell.

scenes.visual: Return to fly brain lineages. Compare Prospero loss in a ganglion mother cell with Brat loss mainly in a type II intermediate progenitor that fails to mature. Show the normal type II sequence: neuroblast produces an intermediate progenitor, which makes ganglion mother cells through several divisions. Beside it show expanding self-renewing cells after fate-control failure. Do not depict every polarity defect as inevitably causing a tumour.

scenes.tts: In mammals, the division plane predicts fate less reliably. The fly rule is clear. Polarity and spindle alignment sort the cargo. One daughter keeps the stem cell going. The other moves toward differentiation.

scenes.visual: Briefly label the mammalian boundary: division plane predicts fate less reliably. Finish with the normal type I fly sequence: apical-basal polarity, aligned spindle, basal cargo inheritance, retained neuroblast and differentiating ganglion mother cell lineage. End on renewal plus output, replacing the old Numb-only rule.
End card: Asymmetric division keeps a neural stem cell while producing differentiating progeny.
